response: Write a=k^alpha, b=k^beta, and c=k^gamma, where alpha, beta, and gamma are nonnegative integers (the argument is unchanged if powers are required to have positive exponents). A quadratic has exactly one real root precisely when its discriminant is zero, so k^(2beta)=4k^(alpha+gamma). Since k=1 would give 1=4, we have k>1. Hence k^(2beta-alpha-gamma)=4. The exponent on the left must be positive, and the only ways an integral power of an integer k>1 can equal 4 are k=2 with exponent 2, or k=4 with exponent 1. The repeated root is r=b/(2a)=k^(beta-alpha)/2. If k=2, then r=2^(beta-alpha-1), so among such values below 100 the largest is 64, since 64<100<128. If k=4, then r=4^(beta-alpha)/2; the largest such value below 100 is 32, since the next one is 128. Thus r cannot exceed 64. This value is attainable: take k=2, alpha=1, beta=8, and gamma=13. Then (a,b,c)=(2,256,8192), the discriminant is 256^2-4(2)(8192)=0, and the repeated root is 256/(2·2)=64. Therefore the maximum possible value of r is 64.

For every polynomial with integer coefficients and every pair of integers u and v, the difference f(u)-f(v) is divisible by u-v. Indeed, for each nonnegative integer t, u^t-v^t is divisible by u-v, and the assertion follows by taking the corresponding integer linear combination. Applying this with u=2010 and v=2008 shows that 2 divides f(2010)-f(2008). The assumed values would make this difference 1867-0=1867, which is odd. This contradiction proves that no such polynomial exists.

Let P(x,y) denote the given equation, and put c=f(0) and d=ac. First, f is injective: if f(u)=f(v), then for any y the left sides of P(u,y) and P(v,y) are equal, while their right sides are af(y)+u and af(y)+v, so u=v. Also, P(x,0) gives f(f(x))=x+d. Apply f to both sides of the original equation. Using the last identity on its left side yields f(x+af(y))=f(x)+ay+d. If z=f(y), then f(z)=y+d, so y=f(z)-d. Consequently, for all rational x and z, f(x+az)=f(x)+af(z)+(1-a)d. Since a is nonzero, every rational h can be written as az. Thus f(x+h)-f(x) is independent of x. Taking x=0 identifies this difference as f(h)-c, and therefore g(x)=f(x)-c satisfies g(x+h)=g(x)+g(h) for all rational x,h. Every additive function from Q to Q is multiplication by a rational constant: if p=g(1), additivity first gives g(n)=np for integers n and then g(m/n)=(m/n)p. Hence f(x)=px+c. Substitution into the original equation gives p^2=1 and c(p+1-a)=0. If p=-1, the second relation is -ac=0, so c=0 because a is nonzero, giving f(x)=-x. If p=1, it gives c(2-a)=0, so f(x)=x for every a, and when a=2 one may in fact choose any c in Q, obtaining f(x)=x+c. Direct substitution verifies all these functions. Therefore, for a not equal to 2 the solutions are f(x)=x and f(x)=-x; for a=2 the solutions are f(x)=-x and f(x)=x+c for arbitrary rational c.

For each element t of {1,2,...,2019}, count the n-tuples for which t belongs to the union. There are 2^(2019n) n-tuples altogether, because each of the n sets may be chosen in 2^2019 ways. If t belongs to none of A_1,...,A_n, each A_i must be a subset of the other 2018 elements, giving 2^(2018n) tuples. Thus t is in the union for exactly 2^(2019n)-2^(2018n) tuples. Now count pairs consisting of a tuple and an element of its union. Counting first by tuples gives the sum in the problem, while counting first by the 2019 possible elements gives 2019(2^(2019n)-2^(2018n)). Hence the required sum is 2019·2^(2018n)(2^n-1).

Write a=n+u and b=m+v, where n and m are integers and 0≤u,v<1. Then floor(a)=n and floor(b)=m, so the given equality becomes 2n+u=2m+v. Rearranging gives 2(n-m)=v-u. The left side is an even integer, whereas -1<v-u<1. The only integer in this open interval is 0, so n=m. The same equation then gives u=v. Therefore a=n+u=m+v=b.

Use the tangent subtraction identity. If a_n=tan(theta), then (sqrt(3)a_n-1)/(a_n+sqrt(3))=tan(theta-pi/6). Since a_0=1=tan(pi/4), induction gives a_n=tan(pi/4-npi/6). The recurrence denominators do not vanish along this sequence: a denominator could vanish only if pi/4-npi/6 were congruent to -pi/3 modulo pi, which after multiplication by 12 would require 2n to be congruent to 7 modulo 12, an impossibility. Because tangent has period pi, the sequence has period 6. Since 2017 is congruent to 1 modulo 6, a_2017=a_1=(sqrt(3)-1)/(sqrt(3)+1)=2-sqrt(3). Thus a=2, b=-1, and c=3, so a+b+c=4.

Write every number below 2024 in base 17. Since 2023=7·17^2, the available digit vectors are (h,u,v) with 0≤h≤6 and 0≤u,v≤16, together with the single vector (7,0,0). We take the sequence in increasing order, as required for the binomial coefficients binom(a_i,a_j) with i>j; equality cannot occur because binom(t,t)=1. Lucas's theorem says that binom(N,K) is nonzero modulo 17 exactly when every base-17 digit of K is at most the corresponding digit of N. Thus a valid collection is an antichain under componentwise comparison of its digit vectors. Consider first the box B={0,...,6}×{0,...,16}×{0,...,16}, ranked by h+u+v. A product of finite chains has a symmetric chain decomposition: this follows inductively from the corresponding decomposition of a rectangular grid, by pairing ranks equidistant from the middle. Consequently every antichain in B meets each symmetric chain at most once and has size at most the largest rank level. The rank-generating polynomial is (1+x+...+x^6)(1+x+...+x^16)^2; it is symmetric and unimodal, so its largest coefficient is at rank 19. For h=0,1,...,6, the numbers of pairs (u,v) with u+v=19-h are respectively 14,15,16,17,16,15,14, whose sum is 107. Hence B has width 107. Adding the one remaining vector (7,0,0) can increase an antichain by at most one, so m≤108. To attain 108, take all 107 vectors in B whose digit sum is 19, and also take (7,0,0), then list their represented integers increasingly. Distinct vectors of digit sum 19 are incomparable. Moreover each has u+v>0, so it is not componentwise at most (7,0,0). Lucas's theorem therefore makes every required binomial coefficient divisible by 17. Thus the largest possible value of m is 108.

Let r_i be the number of marbles in row i and c_j the number in column j. There are 33 marbles, so the sums of the ten row counts and of the ten column counts are both 33. An empty square in row i and column j receives the number r_i+c_j. Summing the row contributions over empty squares gives sum_i r_i(10-r_i), and summing the column contributions gives sum_j c_j(10-c_j). Therefore the total written sum is 660-sum_i r_i^2-sum_j c_j^2. Among ten nonnegative integers with sum 33, the sum of squares is minimized when no two differ by more than one: if two differed by at least two, moving one unit from the larger to the smaller would decrease the sum of squares. Hence the minimum occurs with three counts equal to 4 and seven equal to 3, and it is 3·16+7·9=111. Applying this separately to rows and columns gives an upper bound of 660-111-111=438. This bound is attainable. Number rows and columns modulo 10, and initially put marbles in columns i,i+1,i+2 of row i for every i; this gives three marbles in every row and column. Add marbles at (0,3), (1,4), and (2,5). These squares were empty, and now exactly three rows and three columns have four marbles while all others have three. Thus the written sum is 438, which is the maximum.
